definition: Vociferous means loud with voices; noisily outspoken.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word vociferous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know vociferous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Trivia night turned vociferous at the final question, both teams shouting rulebook passages over the quizmaster's bell.
Outspoken says its piece plainly, at any volume; vociferous says it at the top of its lungs.
Thunderous goes past vociferous — the voices have merged into weather, and no single word survives the roar.

Clamorous is a din with voices in it — shouts, calls, and noise all tangled together, the sound of a crowd wanting things at once. Vociferous is narrower and more pointed: its voices mean what they shout. A clamorous room is loud with people; a vociferous one is loud with opinions.

Noisy is the broadest loudness word there is: it covers any loud sound at all, voiced or not — engines, machinery, weather, waves. Vociferous is loudness made specifically of human voices saying things. Every vociferous crowd is noisy; a noisy machine can never be vociferous.

Every stall calls its prices over the next stall's prices; a vociferous dispute about scale weights is refought at full volume each Tuesday; and when the mackerel boat is late, three hundred voices tell the harbor about it together.
First-time visitors stand at the gate and brace, as if against weather.

Vociferous is the exact word because it is loudness made of voices — the Latin roots literally mean 'voice-carrying.' A jackhammer can rattle windows but is never vociferous; the market is, because its noise is people saying things at volume: prices, gripes, opinions.
Loud, boisterous, and above all voiced.
Vociferous is loudness with language in it — picket lines, fans, gripes, anything shouted and meant.
Its unit-mate vehemently measures the feeling behind an expression, which can stay quiet; vociferous measures the decibels of actual voices.
For noise without voices — engines, horns, surf — reach for plain loud or earsplitting instead.

When the station announced it was dropping the overnight jazz show, it expected a few sad emails.
Instead the show's listeners proved vociferous beyond anything in the station's history.
They rang the request line until it crashed, read prepared statements at the public board meeting, and chanted the host's name outside the studio window.
The station manager noted that the noise never blurred: every shout was a sentence, and every sentence made the same demand.
The show returned within a month, moved one hour earlier, with its host reading the loudest of the protest letters on air.
